title: Fulford Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Fulford wells have a 180-foot median depth; see local yields, water levels, permit history, and drilling costs.
h1: Fulford, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land around Fulford means planning for a mountain well in fractured bedrock. Records within 8 miles show a median completed depth of 180 feet, but the spread is wide: the middle half runs from 98 to 300 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 940 feet.

Reported production is generally strong in this local record, with a 15.0 gpm median yield. That does not guarantee the result on a particular lot. A permit record is a useful starting point, not a substitute for a site-specific well investigation, permit review, and realistic construction budget.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Fulford?
sections.html:
Fulford’s permitted wells are mostly moderate-depth wells, but mountain geology creates a broad bidding range. 25% are under 100 feet, while 49% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Another 22% reach between 300 and 600 feet, and 4% are deeper than 600 feet.

For a driller’s estimate, the 180-foot median is a planning point rather than a promise. A site near the middle of the local data may support a standard-depth bid, but a lot requiring a hole near the upper part of the 98-to-300-foot middle half will carry more drilling, casing, grout, and development exposure. Fractured granite and gneiss can change depth quickly from one property to the next.

sections.heading: What well yield can a Fulford buyer expect?
sections.html:
The available yield records are unusually favorable: the median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gpm. The record shows 79% of reported wells producing more than 15 gpm, while 20% fall between 5 and 15 gpm. Only 1% are in the 1-to-5-gpm range, and none are recorded below 1 gpm.

That is encouraging for household planning, but it is based on 164 wells reporting a pump yield, not every permitted well. Ask for the actual well construction report and pump test for nearby properties. Storage tanks can help smooth peak household demand, but they do not turn a low-producing well into a high-producing one.

sections.heading: Is the water table changing near Fulford?
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 56 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 22 to 85 feet. Only 49 records include a static water level, so the data is a limited local sample rather than a complete groundwater trend.

The decade series does not show a simple dropping water table in these records. Median depth to water was 82 feet in the 1990s, 32 feet in the 2010s, and 25 feet in the 2020s. In other words, the reported measurements became shallower over time. Differences in well locations, measurement conditions, and reporting may explain part of that change. Treat the current nearby static levels as a comparison point, not a guarantee for an unbuilt lot.

sections.heading: Who has drilled Fulford wells, and when?
sections.html:
Permit history is concentrated in the 1990s, when 288 permits were issued in the local record. The record also includes 92 permits from the 2000s, 74 from the 1980s, 62 from the 2010s, and 38 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. There are 640 wells in the Colorado DWR permit record, with 270 recorded as constructed.

Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, listed with Shelton and Joe Wayne, appears most often with 225 records. Shelton Drilling Corporation, listed with Shelton and Wayne, appears on 46. Authorized, listed as Pe and Pg, appears on 23. Use these names as permit-history clues, then confirm current licensing, availability, and scope directly before selecting a contractor.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Fulford?
sections.html:
Local drilling is priced for fractured mountain bedrock, described in the cost model as granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the local 180-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $11,700 to $18,000.

A finished system costs more than the hole. With a pump, tank, trenching, and electrical included, the modeled total at that depth is about $17,700 to $30,000. A bid should state what is included, including casing, grout, well development, testing, mobilization, trenching, and electrical work. If the driller has to continue toward the local 462-foot 90th percentile, the drilling portion can move well beyond a median-depth allowance. Get a written depth assumption and a clear change-order rate.

sections.heading: What risks should Fulford buyers check?
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 38 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove contamination on a particular parcel, but they justify a records review and water-quality testing before closing.

Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, covering 635 wells. Only 2 name the Mancos and 1 names an alluvial aquifer. Ask about casing and grout, well construction, pump testing, and a certified drinking-water test. Also confirm septic setbacks, drainfield space, access for a rig, and whether the building site can support trenching and utilities. Domestic use may require the correct DWR permit, and an augmentation plan can matter in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Fulford lot
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring wells, not the most optimistic number in a listing. Compare depth, static water level, yield, aquifer description, construction date, and reported use. The local use mix is 58% domestic or household, 9% irrigation, 4% stock, and 23% monitoring, so make sure the records you compare serve a purpose similar to yours.

Before closing, have a Colorado water professional review the DWR permit and confirm that the proposed home, number of residences, fixtures, and any irrigation plan fit the permit terms. For a new build, price the access driveway, drilling contingency, pump system, electrical service, septic system, and water testing together. Fulford is near Edwards, Avon, Eagle, Wolcott, Norrie, and Minturn, but a closer well record is usually more useful than a general regional average.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Fulford, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 8 miles of Fulford is 180 feet. The middle half runs from 98 to 300 feet. About 25% are under 100 feet, 49% are between 100 and 300 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 940 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss can make depth vary sharply between neighboring lots.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Fulford?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 180-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $11,700 to $18,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $17,700 to $30,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added site work can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Fulford wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 164 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gpm. The middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gpm, with 79% reporting more than 15 gpm. Records show 20% between 5 and 15 gpm, 1% between 1 and 5 gpm, and none under 1 gpm. Nearby test results remain more useful than the overall median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Fulford?
faq.a: A permit record does not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 38 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well through a qualified laboratory before occupancy, and review local environmental records. The nearby mapped sites are reasons to test, not proof that a specific well is contaminated.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Fulford?
faq.a: The available static-water records do not show a simple drop. Median depth to water was 82 feet below the surface in the 1990s, 32 feet in the 2010s, and 25 feet in the 2020s. Only 49 wells report static water levels, and measurements come from different locations and conditions. Use nearby current measurements as a comparison, not a guarantee for a new well.
